target.title: Plantinga and Ash‘arites on Divine Simplicity
target.thesis: The objection that no distinction can be drawn within God, so that divine attributes cannot be distinguished from God's essence, is inconsistent with the doctrine of divine simplicity, and the reductio arguments against simplicity (Plantinga, Baghdādī, Taftāzānī) rest on a mistaken presumption of such a distinction.

objections.text: Consider a lab with one sealed, perfectly calibrated instrument, the Gauge G, whose single dial reads a single value. Ask: how many 'properties' does G have? Its reading, its calibration, and its sensitivity to pressure all seem distinct, yet each is just the same physical state of one mechanism, described under different counterfactual and relational aspects. Now transpose: suppose a simple being S whose essence is pure act. Omnipotence is 'S can bring about any possible effect'; omniscience is 'S's knowledge is adequate to all truths'; omnibenevolence is 'S's will is directed to the good'. Each description picks out S under a different range of possible outcomes or relations to creatures. The plurality in c005 comes from the grammar of predication and from our finite concepts, not from any difference in what S is. So the premise's inference, from 'these attributes are multiple in our description' to 'they are multiple' and hence 'not identical', fails: the multiplicity is epistemic and conceptual, not ontological. The claim that all attributes are identical is therefore not shown hard to accept by the mere plurality of attribute terms.
objections.premise_fails_because: Premise c005 treats the plurality of attribute terms (omnipotence, omniscience, omnibenevolence) as evidence of real multiplicity in God, but that plurality is at most conceptual and grammatical, so it cannot ground the claim that identity of attributes is hard to accept.

objections.text: The premise assumes that because God is identical to the divine essence, and properties are abstract objects, God must be abstract. But it equivocates on "property." In the claim "properties are abstract objects," property means a general universal, repeatable and non-subsistent. In divine simplicity, God is identical to His own essence: a singular, concrete, subsistent particular, not a repeatable universal. The premise needs the divine essence to be an abstract object, yet it only establishes that God is identical to His own essence. It never shows that this particular essence is abstract in the way general properties are. Without that missing step, the inference that God becomes an abstract object collapses. The premise trades on treating a unique concrete reality as if it were a general abstract universal.
objections.premise_fails_because: Premise W3115675310.c006 fails because it equivocates between general abstract properties and God's singular concrete essence, skipping the required proof that this particular essence is itself an abstract object.

objections.text: Consider trope theory, where properties are particularized, concrete entities rather than abstract universals. The redness of a specific apple is a concrete particular, not an abstract object. Now suppose divine simplicity identifies God with the divine essence, and the divine essence is a trope—a concrete, particularized property rather than a universal. On this view, God is identical to a concrete particular property, not an abstract object. God remains concrete, causally active, and capable of intentional action. A trope can be instantiated once and bear causal relations, so there is no entailment from 'God is identical to a property' to 'God is an abstract object.' The premise only follows if one assumes a Platonic universal theory of properties, where all properties are abstract, but this is not the only available metaphysics of properties. The move from 'God is a property' to 'God is abstract' requires an unstated and contestable assumption about the nature of properties.
objections.premise_fails_because: Premise W3115675310.c006 fails because it assumes all properties are abstract objects, but trope theory provides concrete particular properties, so divine simplicity can identify God with a concrete property rather than an abstract object.

objections.text: In metallurgy, a single substance like steel can exhibit multiple distinct properties—hardness, ductility, resistance to corrosion—each irreducible to the others yet all grounded in its unified essence. Similarly, a divine essence could manifest as distinct attributes without collapsing them into identity, just as a prism refracts a single beam of light into separate colors. The premise assumes that unity of source necessitates identity of effects, but this overlooks how a single origin can yield plural, non-identical expressions.
objections.premise_fails_because: W3115675310.c004 fails because unity of essence does not logically require identity of distinct attributes.

objections.text: c006 claims divine simplicity makes God an abstract object rather than a personal creator, because properties are abstract objects. This smuggles in the assumption that identity with a property automatically places the bearer in the category 'abstract object.' But divine simplicity only says attributes are identical to essence; it says nothing about whether the resulting simple reality is concrete or abstract. A theist can hold that God's omnipotence, omniscience, and omnibenevolence are identical to one undivided essence, and that this essence is a concrete, acting, personal being who creates, sustains, and responds. The premise needs the extra thesis that 'being a property' entails 'being abstract' to generate its absurd consequence, but that thesis is a separate metaphysical commitment (that all properties are abstracta) foreign to divine simplicity itself. Without it, the inference from 'attributes are identical to essence' to 'God is an abstract object' simply does not follow. The argument cannot both deny this extra thesis (as a theist would) and use it to produce the absurdity it needs.
objections.premise_fails_because: W3115675310.c006 fails because it smuggles in the independent metaphysical thesis that all properties are abstract objects, a commitment divine simplicity does not entail, so the inference from attribute-identity to abstractness is invalid.

objections.text: Consider a theologian, Emma, who believes divine simplicity is false but still worthy of consideration due to its historical significance and the potential for new insights. Emma's intention is to understand the concept better, not to reject it outright. In her research, she encounters various interpretations of divine simplicity, some of which seem more plausible than others. Emma's belief that divine simplicity is false does not automatically lead her to reject it, as she values the intellectual exercise of exploring its implications.
objections.premise_fails_because: The hidden premise fails because it assumes that considering divine simplicity as false necessarily means rejecting it, which is not the case for individuals like Emma who approach the concept with a more nuanced perspective.

objections.text: Father Thomas, a Thomist priest, teaches that God’s essence is simple: it is actus essendi, a concrete participation in being, not a collection of abstract properties. In his parish, a believer asks why God can love and create personally if simplicity makes Him an abstract object. Thomas explains that simplicity affirms God’s unity of act, not His lack of personality: the same simple essence is the source of divine love, power, and knowledge. When the believer prays, she experiences God’s personal response, confirming that God operates as a personal creator, not as a detached abstract. This lived example shows that divine simplicity does not entail God’s abstractness, contradicting premise c006.
objections.premise_fails_because: Premise c006 fails because Thomist classical theism holds that divine simplicity denotes a simple, concrete essence, preserving God’s personal creator nature, not making Him an abstract object.

objections.text: A saint participates in the uncreated light of God. This light is not the unknowable essence of God, yet it is truly God. God is simple in His essence, but He communicates Himself through distinct, uncreated energies. When we speak of His love, His justice, or His power, we are describing these divine energies. These energies are distinct from the essence, yet they are not separate from God. They provide multiplicity in how God acts and is known without compromising His essential unity. Divine attributes correspond to these energies rather than the essence itself, preserving both simplicity and the reality of distinct divine properties.
objections.premise_fails_because: W3115675310.c003 fails because divine simplicity does not necessitate that all attributes are identical to the essence, as God possesses distinct, uncreated energies.

objections.text: A scholar believes that a single entity can be described using multiple distinct terms without those terms implying the existence of multiple entities. For instance, one individual can be described as both a 'father' and a 'doctor.' While these descriptions are conceptually different, they both refer to the same underlying person. Similarly, 'omnipotence' and 'omniscience' can be distinct ways for humans to conceptualize the one divine essence. The ability to use different words to describe God does not necessitate that the attributes are ontologically separate. Therefore, c005 fails because it assumes that the conceptual plurality of attributes necessitates an ontological plurality.
objections.premise_fails_because: c005 fails because it assumes that the conceptual plurality of attributes necessitates an ontological plurality.

objections.text: Consider a community of theologians who independently derive two characterizations of God: one through reflection on divine power (omnipotence), another through reflection on divine knowledge (omniscience). These are genuinely distinct conceptual achievements, reached through different epistemic routes, with different explanatory roles. The theologians can distinguish the concepts, apply them separately, and even wonder whether a single being could satisfy both. Now suppose divine simplicity is true and the attributes are ontologically identical. The conceptual multiplicity remains a real datum: the two concepts are not interchangeable, and the fact that both apply to the same being is non-trivial and demands explanation. Yet this multiplicity is not ontological—there is no difference in being between the attributes. The distinctness lies in sense and cognitive role, not in reality. The premise claims only ontological multiplicity yields a datum simplicity must address, but here conceptual multiplicity itself constitutes a datum requiring account, even with no ontological difference.
objections.premise_fails_because: Premise W3115675310.arg1.r1 fails because conceptual multiplicity—distinct concepts with different epistemic routes and explanatory roles—can constitute a genuine datum requiring explanation even when there is no ontological multiplicity.

objections.text: Consider a being, Alpha, that exists necessarily and has zero composition—no form/matter, no act/potency, no essence/existence distinction. Alpha's nature simply IS Alpha's act of existing. Alpha consciously deliberates, chooses specific physical constants, and creates a cosmos. On Platonic universals, Alpha is not a universal: universals are repeatable, Alpha is necessarily unique. On trope theory, Alpha is not a trope: tropes are abstract particulars dependent on concrete bearers, while Alpha is self-subsistent and personal. Yet Alpha is simple—divine simplicity holds. The premise frames the issue as: God is identical to a property, and then asks whether that property is a Platonic universal or a trope. But Alpha is a subsistent act of personal existence, not a property under either framework. The property/universal/trope taxonomy simply does not capture what Alpha is. A being whose essence is identical to its existence falls outside the category 'property' altogether.
objections.premise_fails_because: Premise W3115675310.arg1.r2 fails because it assumes divine simplicity entails God is identical to a property, but a being that is pure subsistent existence can be simple without being a property under either Platonic or trope-theoretic frameworks.

objections.text: Imagine a language where the word 'glorb' means 'both omnipotent and omniscient.' In this language, speakers use 'glorb' to refer to a single, unified concept, yet they still distinguish omnipotence and omniscience in practice—e.g., praying for wisdom (omniscience) but not for strength (omnipotence). The semantic premise fails because conceptual multiplicity can exist even if a language lacks separate terms for it.
objections.premise_fails_because: W3115675310.arg1.r3 fails because conceptual distinction does not depend on linguistic separation.

restatements.paper_vocabulary: The objection contends that the multiplicity of divine attributes (omnipotence, omniscience, omnibenevolence) is merely epistemic and conceptual, arising from the grammar of predication and finite concepts, rather than from any ontological plurality in the simple divine essence; so the inference from 'these attributes are multiple in our description' to 'they are really distinct, hence not identical' fails, and c005 does not show that identity of all attributes is hard to accept.
restatements.plain_english: The argument says that because we describe one thing in many different ways, it's wrong to conclude the thing has many separate parts or features. restatements.paper_vocabulary: Objection to W3115675310.arg1.r2: a being whose essence is identical to its act of existence, that is necessary, uniquely self-subsistent and personally agentive, and that consciously chooses and creates, is simple yet is neither a Platonic universal (since it is not repeatable) nor a trope (since it is not an abstract particular dependent on a concrete bearer). So the Platonic/trope taxonomy of properties cannot capture God, and the claim that God is identical to a property, and so faces the personal-creator worry only under one of those two theories, fails because God falls outside the category 'property' altogether.
restatements.plain_english: Imagine a being that has no parts, no mix of possibility and actuality, and no gap between what it is and that it exists, and that also thinks, chooses, and makes the universe. It is not a general quality that many things could share, and it is not a quality that depends on some thing it belongs to. So the claim that God must be some kind of property, and so the question is only which kind, is wrong: such a being is not a property at all, so the sorting of properties into two kinds misses what it is.
restatements.neighboring_tradition: In philosophy of religion and analytic theism, this is the move that a personal, self-existing God is not a 'thing' in the ontological category the sorting presupposes, so the classification of divine attributes into abstract types leaves out the personal being it purports to classify. It parallels the complaint in the problem of evil and divine hiddenness debates that a standard theistic model is being judged by categories that do not apply to a personal agent, and the familiar charge in the Euthyphro-style and anti-reductive debates that God cannot be fitted into a generic kind of entity.

No reply was received: the defense failed validation three times, so nothing in the record answers the objection. It therefore stands as a challenge to c005 and to the inference from "these attributes are multiple in our description" to "they are multiple." That inference needs an ontological premise, and the plurality of predicates does not supply one. The Gauge case shows that one physical state can support many distinct descriptions.

You may reply that the modal profiles differ objectively: omnipotence concerns possible effects, omniscience concerns truths, and these ranges are not the same. But if those profiles are grounded in S's nature, then S has distinct features, and simplicity is threatened only if those features are distinct in being. You owe an argument that the difference in relational or counterfactual role is a difference in what S is. Without that, c005 has not shown that the attributes are non-identical, and the argument's case for rejecting simplicity remains unsupported at this step.

rounds.speaker: defender_a
rounds.content:
You are right that plurality of predicates alone does not establish plurality in being, and the Gauge case shows one state can ground many descriptions. You press me to show that the modal and relational profiles you list are differences in what S is. I concede I have not shown that. The attribute-as-sense reply [W7172336769.c036] can be made: the many attributes are different senses of one referent, compatible with simplicity. [W4229080938.c048] suggests the difference between knowing the self and knowing its relation to another tracks a difference in the possible, not merely in our concepts, but that is a claim about modal profile, not yet about being. So the simplicist can hold that the profiles are grounded in one essence. The opponent must then press whether sense-difference is enough, and the Spinozist worry [W4239883184.a1] about many attributes implying many substances is where that pressure bites. Your objection therefore stands against c005 as written. Final position: the argument does not survive at this step. It needs the premise that multiplicity of divine attributes is ontologically real, not merely conceptual or relational, since only real multiplicity makes non-identity a datum that simplicity must deny.

Revised premise: Multiplicity of divine attributes must be ontologically real (differences in being, not only in sense or description), since only real multiplicity makes the attributes' non-identity a datum that simplicity must deny.

rounds.content:
You are right that distinct attribute terms do not by themselves entail distinct properties [W7172336769.c035], but your Gauge G analogy fails because a gauge’s calibration and sensitivity are merely relational aspects of one physical state, whereas omniscience and omnipotence are defined by formally distinct objects and causal profiles. While [W7172336769.c036] rightly uses Frege’s sense-reference distinction to show that ‘good’ and ‘wise’ can share the same referent, this does not establish that the attributes themselves, as defined by their distinct formal objects, can be identical without collapsing the very differences that make them theologically significant. Your objection therefore lands partly against c005 as it stands, because the premise leaves room for a purely conceptual reading of the multiplicity it cites.

rounds.speaker: referee
rounds.content: Not a misreading: The objection directly attacks premise W3115675310.c006 as stated. The premise claims that divine simplicity implies God is an abstract object 'since properties are abstract objects.' The objection challenges this very assumption by arguing that properties need not be abstract objects—trope theory offers a metaphysics where properties are concrete particulars. This is a direct attack on the premise's reasoning, not an attack on something the argument does not claim.

rounds.speaker: defender_a
rounds.content:
You are right that c006 is a conditional whose force depends on a premise the argument leaves implicit: that properties are abstract objects. The text says 'since properties are abstract objects' as if this were common ground, and that is precisely the assumption you contest. Your trope proposal is a serious option. Trope theorists such as those in the Thomist-friendly camp would say God is identical to a concrete, particular property, and that avoids abstractness. [W7172336769.c019] gives a related Thomist line: God is Life itself and not a thing, nature, or abstract property, so God can act, know, and will. That supports your point that the abstractness conclusion is not forced by simplicity alone.

But the objection does not fully rescue the personal-creator worry. A trope is a particular, and a particular property instantiated once is still a property, not an agent. [W4229080938.c004] states the worry directly: identifying God with a single property makes God a property rather than a person. Trope theory changes the ontological category from abstract to concrete, but the worry that God is a property, not a subject who knows and wills, is not dissolved by changing the category. [W3115675310.c023] presents the personal-creator objection as applying to any identification of God with a property, which your move does not address.

So c006 as stated does not survive unchanged. The defensible repair is to weaken the premise, not to deny that simplicity raises a problem.

Revised premise: Divine simplicity implies God is identical to a property, and if that property is an abstract universal then God is an abstract object, so the personal-creator worry holds only under a Platonic theory of properties, while on trope theory it reappears as the question whether a single instantiated property can be a personal agent.

rounds.speaker: defender_b
rounds.content:
You are right that the assumption is explicit, not tacit [W3115675310.c006], and your trope-theoretic counterexample shows that the inference to abstractness is theory-dependent. The argument channels Plantinga's claim that if God is identical with each property, God is a property and an abstract object who cannot be a personal creator [W3115675310.c023]. A trope theorist blocks the 'abstract object' step, since tropes are concrete. Still, the deeper worry survives: if God is identical with a single property—universal or trope—then God is a property rather than a person [W4229080938.c004]. The trope theorist now owes an account of how a single property-particular can also be the distinct, rich person of monotheism, and your example of a causally active trope does not yet show that a property-particular can be a person. Nevertheless, because the premise asserts unqualifiedly that properties are abstract objects, the argument overreaches. I concede that the premise must be narrowed.

rounds.speaker: referee
rounds.content: Not a misreading: The premise (W3115675310.arg1.r1) explicitly claims that ONLY ontological multiplicity makes the attributes' non-identity a datum that simplicity must deny. The objection directly attacks this 'only' claim by arguing that conceptual multiplicity also constitutes a datum requiring explanation, even absent ontological difference. This is a straightforward challenge to the premise as stated, not an attack on something the argument does not claim.

rounds.speaker: defender_a
rounds.content: The argument as stated, through r1, claims that only ontological multiplicity is a datum simplicity must deny, and you are right that a conceptual multiplicity datum exists. But notice what it does to the argument. Your theologians' two concepts are genuinely distinct, and the fact that one being satisfies both is non-trivial. Simplicity can accommodate this without contradiction, as the Fregean reply in [W7172336769.c036] suggests: 'good' and 'wise' share a referent and differ in sense. So the conceptual datum is real but is explained by sense-difference, not by a failure of simplicity. That is exactly why r1 needs the ontological qualifier. The argument's target is the claim that the attributes are non-identical in being, and only that claim collides with simplicity. Your case shows that conceptual multiplicity is a datum simplicity can absorb, which supports the restriction rather than undermining it. The residual worry is whether the sense-reference explanation is adequate: al-Fārābī's view that God is free of semantic as well as ontological multiplicity [W2972751537.a1] would have to be defended, since it is a substantive commitment. But that is a challenge to the Fregean story, not a refutation of r1. The argument survives with r1 as stated, provided one grants that the conceptual datum is discharged by sense differences.

rounds.speaker: attacker
rounds.content: You concede that conceptual multiplicity is a real datum but say simplicity can discharge it via the Fregean sense-reference model, so r1's ontological restriction is justified. The problem is that the Fregean discharge is not cost-free. In standard cases like "morning star" and "evening star," the two senses are different modes of presenting the same referent. But "omnipotent" and "omniscient" don't merely present one property differently—they appear to *predicate* different things: power versus knowledge. The sense difference is a difference in what is attributed, not just in how it is presented. So the Fregean model doesn't straightforwardly apply: it presupposes that these senses are merely different routes to one property, which is exactly what the simplicity theorist needs to establish, not assume. The conceptual datum thus forces a substantive, contestable commitment rather than a clean discharge. r1's dismissal of non-ontological multiplicity remains too quick.

rounds.speaker: defender_a
rounds.content: Your rejoinder is right that 'omnipotent' and 'omniscient' do not look like mere alternative routes to one property, and I grant that the Fregean discharge is not automatic. But two things remain. First, the datum you describe is a datum about concepts and their epistemic roles, and simplicity can explain it by saying the concepts are distinct while their referent is one; the theologians' inability to see at once that one being satisfies both is exactly what sense-difference predicts, as in the 'good' and 'wise' case [W7172336769.c036]. Second, the predication worry bears on whether the sense is a difference in what is attributed, and that is a question about the semantics of divine predication, which the simplicity tradition has long debated, as Ibn Rushd's treatment of the verbal and conceptual differences between theologians and philosophers suggests [W7119078330.a1]. A contestable semantic commitment is a cost, but it is not a demonstration that simplicity fails. So I hold that r1 survives the objection on its stated scope: the argument's collision claim concerns non-identity in being. What the objection shows is that the argument needs an explicit semantic premise to block the stronger charge that conceptual multiplicity is itself a datum simplicity must deny. I concede that the argument as stated does not cover that stronger charge, and I state the premise it would need below.
rounds.revised_premise: Divine attribute-terms have distinct senses whose difference consists in modes of presentation of one simple referent, not in distinct things predicated of God.

rounds.speaker: referee

rounds.speaker: defender_b
rounds.content: You misread our premise if you think it denies the reality of your theologians' conceptual achievements. We do not claim that conceptual multiplicity is unreal; we claim it is not the kind of multiplicity that generates a conflict with simplicity. Divine simplicity is an ontological thesis about God's essence, not a semantic thesis about our concepts. Your distinct concepts of omnipotence and omniscience can be different senses that share one simple referent, which is precisely how proponents of simplicity defuse the multiplicity objection using Frege's sense-reference distinction [W7172336769.c036]. Indeed, historical disputes about divine attributes are often merely conceptual and terminological [W7119078330.a1]. Because simplicity can swallow conceptual multiplicity whole by treating it as variation in sense rather than in being, the reductio in c005 would collapse unless the multiplicity is located in reality itself. That is exactly why arg1.r1 insists on ontological multiplicity: only a difference in being yields a datum that simplicity cannot explain away. Your example therefore does not undermine the argument; it illustrates why the argument must demand ontological multiplicity to avoid being defused by the sense-reference distinction.

rounds.speaker: attacker
rounds.content: You say simplicity "swallows conceptual multiplicity whole" via sense-reference, but you've only announced the swallowing, not shown it works. Sense-reference handles cases like Hesperus and Phosphorus—two names, one object, different modes of presentation. But omnipotence and omniscience aren't merely different labels; they carry distinct explanatory commitments. Omnipotence explains God's creative power; omniscience explains God's knowledge. If these are one simple property, what accounts for the difference in explanatory role? Sense-reference explains how two concepts share a referent, not why one referent satisfies the different conditions those concepts express. Your reply concedes that conceptual multiplicity requires a theoretical response from the simplicity theorist. Whether that response succeeds is exactly what's at issue—r1 can't settle it by stipulating that only ontological multiplicity counts as a datum.

rounds.speaker: defender_b
rounds.content:
You are right that I announced the Fregean swallowing without showing it can digest distinct explanatory roles. Sense-reference explains co-reference, not how one simple reality satisfies the heterogeneous conditions associated with omnipotence and omniscience. Medieval thinkers recognized genuine tensions between simplicity and multiplicity of attributes, action, and language [W7107962549.a1], and your theologians' case exposes exactly that: the difference is not merely nominal but involves distinct explanatory commitments. I concede that r1 was too narrow in restricting the threatening datum to ontological multiplicity alone. Conceptual multiplicity that includes irreducibly distinct satisfaction conditions and explanatory roles is itself a datum that simplicity must accommodate, and simply labeling it a difference in sense does not obviously discharge that burden.

Revised premise: The distinct satisfaction conditions and explanatory roles of divine attributes constitute a datum that divine simplicity must explain, and the Fregean sense-reference distinction alone cannot discharge that explanatory burden without ontological complexity.

rounds.content:
You are right that r2 takes 'God is identical to a property' as its starting point, and the Alpha case shows that this starting point is not neutral. Alpha is a self-subsisting act of existence, and if that is not a property, then the dilemma in r2 does not even get started for Alpha. But I think the objection proves less than it appears to. The argument's target is the simplicity theorist, and the simplicity literature itself already concedes that the property framing is a pressure point: Plantinga's reading and the worry that divine simplicity makes God a property rather than a person are raised as objections to the doctrine [W4229080938.c004], and the symmetric-parthood reading tries to avoid the 'God is a property' result by other means [W7212186029.c034]. So the objection is pressing on a question the argument already flags. Still, Alpha is a case the argument does not handle. If God's essence is act of existence rather than a universal or trope, then r2's disjunction is incomplete, and the personal-creator worry does not reduce to a Platonic-versus-trope question. That is a genuine gap in r2, not a misreading. I therefore cannot save r2 as stated. The central c006 consequence, that God is an abstract object, still holds on the Platonic horn, but only as a claim about one ontology of properties, not about divine simplicity as such. I concede that the argument as stated does not survive the objection, and the rest of the argument's force rests on c003–c004.

You are right that classical divine simplicity denies the substance-property distinction altogether [W7172336769.c013], but that denial is exactly what generates the ontological puzzle the argument targets. If God is not a substance and not a property, then your 'subsistent act of personal existence' is not a recognized ontological kind—it is either a primitive posit that masks the problem or a trope in disguise. The argument in r2 frames the issue within property theory because once the substance-property boundary is erased, the only available models for understanding a being identical to its attributes are property-like entities such as universals or tropes [W7217702849.a1; W7172336769.c039]. Your Alpha is said to be self-subsistent and personal, yet if Alpha just is his act of existing and is identical to each attribute, we still face the question of how such a being can be a concrete personal agent rather than an abstract or property-like entity [W7212186029.c034]. The classical tradition itself insists that God is his own essence and existence, identical to each attribute, and pure act [W2592965112.a2], but this description does not furnish the metaphysical machinery needed to distinguish Alpha from a causally inert abstractum. The argument's point survives: denying the substance-property distinction does not give God a coherent ontological status as a personal creator; it merely removes the categories that could underwrite that status.

objection.text: Consider a lab with one sealed, perfectly calibrated instrument, the Gauge G, whose single dial reads a single value. Ask: how many 'properties' does G have? Its reading, its calibration, and its sensitivity to pressure all seem distinct, yet each is just the same physical state of one mechanism, described under different counterfactual and relational aspects. Now transpose: suppose a simple being S whose essence is pure act. Omnipotence is 'S can bring about any possible effect'; omniscience is 'S's knowledge is adequate to all truths'; omnibenevolence is 'S's will is directed to the good'. Each description picks out S under a different range of possible outcomes or relations to creatures. The plurality in c005 comes from the grammar of predication and from our finite concepts, not from any difference in what S is. So the premise's inference, from 'these attributes are multiple in our description' to 'they are multiple' and hence 'not identical', fails: the multiplicity is epistemic and conceptual, not ontological. The claim that all attributes are identical is therefore not shown hard to accept by the mere plurality of attribute terms.
objection.premise_fails_because: Premise c005 treats the plurality of attribute terms (omnipotence, omniscience, omnibenevolence) as evidence of real multiplicity in God, but that plurality is at most conceptual and grammatical, so it cannot ground the claim that identity of attributes is hard to accept.

objection.text: The premise assumes that because God is identical to the divine essence, and properties are abstract objects, God must be abstract. But it equivocates on "property." In the claim "properties are abstract objects," property means a general universal, repeatable and non-subsistent. In divine simplicity, God is identical to His own essence: a singular, concrete, subsistent particular, not a repeatable universal. The premise needs the divine essence to be an abstract object, yet it only establishes that God is identical to His own essence. It never shows that this particular essence is abstract in the way general properties are. Without that missing step, the inference that God becomes an abstract object collapses. The premise trades on treating a unique concrete reality as if it were a general abstract universal.
objection.premise_fails_because: Premise W3115675310.c006 fails because it equivocates between general abstract properties and God's singular concrete essence, skipping the required proof that this particular essence is itself an abstract object.

objection.text: Consider trope theory, where properties are particularized, concrete entities rather than abstract universals. The redness of a specific apple is a concrete particular, not an abstract object. Now suppose divine simplicity identifies God with the divine essence, and the divine essence is a trope—a concrete, particularized property rather than a universal. On this view, God is identical to a concrete particular property, not an abstract object. God remains concrete, causally active, and capable of intentional action. A trope can be instantiated once and bear causal relations, so there is no entailment from 'God is identical to a property' to 'God is an abstract object.' The premise only follows if one assumes a Platonic universal theory of properties, where all properties are abstract, but this is not the only available metaphysics of properties. The move from 'God is a property' to 'God is abstract' requires an unstated and contestable assumption about the nature of properties.
objection.premise_fails_because: Premise W3115675310.c006 fails because it assumes all properties are abstract objects, but trope theory provides concrete particular properties, so divine simplicity can identify God with a concrete property rather than an abstract object.

objection.text: In metallurgy, a single substance like steel can exhibit multiple distinct properties—hardness, ductility, resistance to corrosion—each irreducible to the others yet all grounded in its unified essence. Similarly, a divine essence could manifest as distinct attributes without collapsing them into identity, just as a prism refracts a single beam of light into separate colors. The premise assumes that unity of source necessitates identity of effects, but this overlooks how a single origin can yield plural, non-identical expressions.
objection.premise_fails_because: W3115675310.c004 fails because unity of essence does not logically require identity of distinct attributes.

objection.text: c006 claims divine simplicity makes God an abstract object rather than a personal creator, because properties are abstract objects. This smuggles in the assumption that identity with a property automatically places the bearer in the category 'abstract object.' But divine simplicity only says attributes are identical to essence; it says nothing about whether the resulting simple reality is concrete or abstract. A theist can hold that God's omnipotence, omniscience, and omnibenevolence are identical to one undivided essence, and that this essence is a concrete, acting, personal being who creates, sustains, and responds. The premise needs the extra thesis that 'being a property' entails 'being abstract' to generate its absurd consequence, but that thesis is a separate metaphysical commitment (that all properties are abstracta) foreign to divine simplicity itself. Without it, the inference from 'attributes are identical to essence' to 'God is an abstract object' simply does not follow. The argument cannot both deny this extra thesis (as a theist would) and use it to produce the absurdity it needs.
objection.premise_fails_because: W3115675310.c006 fails because it smuggles in the independent metaphysical thesis that all properties are abstract objects, a commitment divine simplicity does not entail, so the inference from attribute-identity to abstractness is invalid.

objection.text: Consider a theologian, Emma, who believes divine simplicity is false but still worthy of consideration due to its historical significance and the potential for new insights. Emma's intention is to understand the concept better, not to reject it outright. In her research, she encounters various interpretations of divine simplicity, some of which seem more plausible than others. Emma's belief that divine simplicity is false does not automatically lead her to reject it, as she values the intellectual exercise of exploring its implications.
objection.premise_fails_because: The hidden premise fails because it assumes that considering divine simplicity as false necessarily means rejecting it, which is not the case for individuals like Emma who approach the concept with a more nuanced perspective.

objection.text: Father Thomas, a Thomist priest, teaches that God’s essence is simple: it is actus essendi, a concrete participation in being, not a collection of abstract properties. In his parish, a believer asks why God can love and create personally if simplicity makes Him an abstract object. Thomas explains that simplicity affirms God’s unity of act, not His lack of personality: the same simple essence is the source of divine love, power, and knowledge. When the believer prays, she experiences God’s personal response, confirming that God operates as a personal creator, not as a detached abstract. This lived example shows that divine simplicity does not entail God’s abstractness, contradicting premise c006.
objection.premise_fails_because: Premise c006 fails because Thomist classical theism holds that divine simplicity denotes a simple, concrete essence, preserving God’s personal creator nature, not making Him an abstract object.

objection.text: A saint participates in the uncreated light of God. This light is not the unknowable essence of God, yet it is truly God. God is simple in His essence, but He communicates Himself through distinct, uncreated energies. When we speak of His love, His justice, or His power, we are describing these divine energies. These energies are distinct from the essence, yet they are not separate from God. They provide multiplicity in how God acts and is known without compromising His essential unity. Divine attributes correspond to these energies rather than the essence itself, preserving both simplicity and the reality of distinct divine properties.
objection.premise_fails_because: W3115675310.c003 fails because divine simplicity does not necessitate that all attributes are identical to the essence, as God possesses distinct, uncreated energies.

objection.text: A scholar believes that a single entity can be described using multiple distinct terms without those terms implying the existence of multiple entities. For instance, one individual can be described as both a 'father' and a 'doctor.' While these descriptions are conceptually different, they both refer to the same underlying person. Similarly, 'omnipotence' and 'omniscience' can be distinct ways for humans to conceptualize the one divine essence. The ability to use different words to describe God does not necessitate that the attributes are ontologically separate. Therefore, c005 fails because it assumes that the conceptual plurality of attributes necessitates an ontological plurality.

objection.text: Consider a community of theologians who independently derive two characterizations of God: one through reflection on divine power (omnipotence), another through reflection on divine knowledge (omniscience). These are genuinely distinct conceptual achievements, reached through different epistemic routes, with different explanatory roles. The theologians can distinguish the concepts, apply them separately, and even wonder whether a single being could satisfy both. Now suppose divine simplicity is true and the attributes are ontologically identical. The conceptual multiplicity remains a real datum: the two concepts are not interchangeable, and the fact that both apply to the same being is non-trivial and demands explanation. Yet this multiplicity is not ontological—there is no difference in being between the attributes. The distinctness lies in sense and cognitive role, not in reality. The premise claims only ontological multiplicity yields a datum simplicity must address, but here conceptual multiplicity itself constitutes a datum requiring account, even with no ontological difference.

On trope theory, Alpha is not a trope: tropes are abstract particulars dependent on concrete bearers, while Alpha is self-subsistent and personal. Yet Alpha is simple—divine simplicity holds. turn.content: Not a misreading: The premise (W3115675310.arg1.r1) explicitly claims that ONLY ontological multiplicity makes the attributes' non-identity a datum that simplicity must deny. The objection directly attacks this 'only' claim by arguing that conceptual multiplicity also constitutes a datum requiring explanation, even absent ontological difference. This is a straightforward challenge to the premise as stated, not an attack on something the argument does not claim.

turn.speaker: referee
turn.content: Not a misreading: The premise W3115675310.arg1.r2 states that 'Divine simplicity implies God is identical to a property.' The objection directly attacks this claim by arguing that a simple being whose essence is identical to its existence is a subsistent act of existence, not a property under either Platonic universalism or trope theory. This is a direct challenge to the premise as stated, not an attack on something the argument does not claim.

turn.speaker: defender_a
turn.content: The argument as stated, through r1, claims that only ontological multiplicity is a datum simplicity must deny, and you are right that a conceptual multiplicity datum exists. But notice what it does to the argument. Your theologians' two concepts are genuinely distinct, and the fact that one being satisfies both is non-trivial. Simplicity can accommodate this without contradiction, as the Fregean reply in [W7172336769.c036] suggests: 'good' and 'wise' share a referent and differ in sense. So the conceptual datum is real but is explained by sense-difference, not by a failure of simplicity. That is exactly why r1 needs the ontological qualifier. The argument's target is the claim that the attributes are non-identical in being, and only that claim collides with simplicity. Your case shows that conceptual multiplicity is a datum simplicity can absorb, which supports the restriction rather than undermining it. The residual worry is whether the sense-reference explanation is adequate: al-Fārābī's view that God is free of semantic as well as ontological multiplicity [W2972751537.a1] would have to be defended, since it is a substantive commitment. But that is a challenge to the Fregean story, not a refutation of r1. The argument survives with r1 as stated, provided one grants that the conceptual datum is discharged by sense differences.

turn.speaker: defender_a
turn.content:
You are right that r2 takes 'God is identical to a property' as its starting point, and the Alpha case shows that this starting point is not neutral. Alpha is a self-subsisting act of existence, and if that is not a property, then the dilemma in r2 does not even get started for Alpha. But I think the objection proves less than it appears to. The argument's target is the simplicity theorist, and the simplicity literature itself already concedes that the property framing is a pressure point: Plantinga's reading and the worry that divine simplicity makes God a property rather than a person are raised as objections to the doctrine [W4229080938.c004], and the symmetric-parthood reading tries to avoid the 'God is a property' result by other means [W7212186029.c034]. So the objection is pressing on a question the argument already flags. Still, Alpha is a case the argument does not handle. If God's essence is act of existence rather than a universal or trope, then r2's disjunction is incomplete, and the personal-creator worry does not reduce to a Platonic-versus-trope question. That is a genuine gap in r2, not a misreading. I therefore cannot save r2 as stated. The central c006 consequence, that God is an abstract object, still holds on the Platonic horn, but only as a claim about one ontology of properties, not about divine simplicity as such. I concede that the argument as stated does not survive the objection, and the rest of the argument's force rests on c003–c004.

Revised premise: Divine simplicity implies God is identical to a property or to a non-property act of existence; if it is a property, then God is an abstract object on the Platonic theory and the personal-creator worry reappears on trope theory, while the act-of-existence option must be separately assessed for whether it can be personal.

turn.speaker: attacker
turn.content: You concede that conceptual multiplicity is a real datum but say simplicity can discharge it via the Fregean sense-reference model, so r1's ontological restriction is justified. The problem is that the Fregean discharge is not cost-free. In standard cases like "morning star" and "evening star," the two senses are different modes of presenting the same referent. But "omnipotent" and "omniscient" don't merely present one property differently—they appear to *predicate* different things: power versus knowledge. The sense difference is a difference in what is attributed, not just in how it is presented. So the Fregean model doesn't straightforwardly apply: it presupposes that these senses are merely different routes to one property, which is exactly what the simplicity theorist needs to establish, not assume. The conceptual datum thus forces a substantive, contestable commitment rather than a clean discharge. r1's dismissal of non-ontological multiplicity remains too quick.

turn.speaker: defender_a
turn.content: Your rejoinder is right that 'omnipotent' and 'omniscient' do not look like mere alternative routes to one property, and I grant that the Fregean discharge is not automatic. But two things remain. First, the datum you describe is a datum about concepts and their epistemic roles, and simplicity can explain it by saying the concepts are distinct while their referent is one; the theologians' inability to see at once that one being satisfies both is exactly what sense-difference predicts, as in the 'good' and 'wise' case [W7172336769.c036]. Second, the predication worry bears on whether the sense is a difference in what is attributed, and that is a question about the semantics of divine predication, which the simplicity tradition has long debated, as Ibn Rushd's treatment of the verbal and conceptual differences between theologians and philosophers suggests [W7119078330.a1]. A contestable semantic commitment is a cost, but it is not a demonstration that simplicity fails. So I hold that r1 survives the objection on its stated scope: the argument's collision claim concerns non-identity in being. What the objection shows is that the argument needs an explicit semantic premise to block the stronger charge that conceptual multiplicity is itself a datum simplicity must deny. I concede that the argument as stated does not cover that stronger charge, and I state the premise it would need below.
turn.revised_premise: Divine attribute-terms have distinct senses whose difference consists in modes of presentation of one simple referent, not in distinct things predicated of God.

turn.speaker: defender_b
turn.content: You misread our premise if you think it denies the reality of your theologians' conceptual achievements. We do not claim that conceptual multiplicity is unreal; we claim it is not the kind of multiplicity that generates a conflict with simplicity. Divine simplicity is an ontological thesis about God's essence, not a semantic thesis about our concepts. Your distinct concepts of omnipotence and omniscience can be different senses that share one simple referent, which is precisely how proponents of simplicity defuse the multiplicity objection using Frege's sense-reference distinction [W7172336769.c036]. Indeed, historical disputes about divine attributes are often merely conceptual and terminological [W7119078330.a1]. Because simplicity can swallow conceptual multiplicity whole by treating it as variation in sense rather than in being, the reductio in c005 would collapse unless the multiplicity is located in reality itself. That is exactly why arg1.r1 insists on ontological multiplicity: only a difference in being yields a datum that simplicity cannot explain away. Your example therefore does not undermine the argument; it illustrates why the argument must demand ontological multiplicity to avoid being defused by the sense-reference distinction.

turn.speaker: defender_b
turn.content:
You are right that classical divine simplicity denies the substance-property distinction altogether [W7172336769.c013], but that denial is exactly what generates the ontological puzzle the argument targets. If God is not a substance and not a property, then your 'subsistent act of personal existence' is not a recognized ontological kind—it is either a primitive posit that masks the problem or a trope in disguise. The argument in r2 frames the issue within property theory because once the substance-property boundary is erased, the only available models for understanding a being identical to its attributes are property-like entities such as universals or tropes [W7217702849.a1; W7172336769.c039]. Your Alpha is said to be self-subsistent and personal, yet if Alpha just is his act of existing and is identical to each attribute, we still face the question of how such a being can be a concrete personal agent rather than an abstract or property-like entity [W7212186029.c034]. The classical tradition itself insists that God is his own essence and existence, identical to each attribute, and pure act [W2592965112.a2], but this description does not furnish the metaphysical machinery needed to distinguish Alpha from a causally inert abstractum. The argument's point survives: denying the substance-property distinction does not give God a coherent ontological status as a personal creator; it merely removes the categories that could underwrite that status.

Revised premise: Divine simplicity denies the substance-property distinction altogether, so God is not a property but falls outside standard ontological categories, and the personal-creator worry reappears as the question whether a being outside the substance-property framework can be a concrete personal agent.

turn.speaker: attacker
turn.content: You say simplicity "swallows conceptual multiplicity whole" via sense-reference, but you've only announced the swallowing, not shown it works. Sense-reference handles cases like Hesperus and Phosphorus—two names, one object, different modes of presentation. But omnipotence and omniscience aren't merely different labels; they carry distinct explanatory commitments. Omnipotence explains God's creative power; omniscience explains God's knowledge. If these are one simple property, what accounts for the difference in explanatory role? Sense-reference explains how two concepts share a referent, not why one referent satisfies the different conditions those concepts express. Your reply concedes that conceptual multiplicity requires a theoretical response from the simplicity theorist. Whether that response succeeds is exactly what's at issue—r1 can't settle it by stipulating that only ontological multiplicity counts as a datum.

turn.speaker: referee
turn.content: revision_required: The objector showed that r2's framing (God is identical to a property, either a Platonic universal or a trope) fails because a simple being like Alpha falls outside the property category altogether. The defender concedes this by acknowledging that classical simplicity denies the substance-property distinction, and saves the argument only by revising the premise to shift the worry from 'is God an abstract property?' to 'can a being outside standard ontological categories be a concrete personal agent?'

turn.speaker: defender_b
turn.content:
You are right that I announced the Fregean swallowing without showing it can digest distinct explanatory roles. Sense-reference explains co-reference, not how one simple reality satisfies the heterogeneous conditions associated with omnipotence and omniscience. Medieval thinkers recognized genuine tensions between simplicity and multiplicity of attributes, action, and language [W7107962549.a1], and your theologians' case exposes exactly that: the difference is not merely nominal but involves distinct explanatory commitments. I concede that r1 was too narrow in restricting the threatening datum to ontological multiplicity alone. Conceptual multiplicity that includes irreducibly distinct satisfaction conditions and explanatory roles is itself a datum that simplicity must accommodate, and simply labeling it a difference in sense does not obviously discharge that burden.

Revised premise: The distinct satisfaction conditions and explanatory roles of divine attributes constitute a datum that divine simplicity must explain, and the Fregean sense-reference distinction alone cannot discharge that explanatory burden without ontological complexity.
